title: Banking: Concurrent Withdrawals

questions.question: Two withdrawals against Rs 5,000
questions.answer:
Account A has Rs 5,000. W1 requests Rs 5,000; W2 requests Rs 10,000. W2 must fail even if it locks the account first. W1 succeeds if no other valid debit consumes the balance. Final balance is Rs 0.

Transactions give atomicity and consistency; row locks isolate competing balance decisions. Commit makes the result durable. Never decide using an unlocked, stale balance.

questions.question: Safe processing sequence
questions.answer:
BEGIN -> lock the persisted withdrawal request -> return its existing outcome if already processed -> lock its account with SELECT FOR UPDATE -> verify account is active, amount is positive and funds are sufficient -> debit -> insert a unique ledger entry -> mark SUCCESS -> COMMIT.

Bind the account and amount to the persisted request, not independently supplied browser parameters. Authorization must happen before processing. A unique (account_id, idempotency_key) prevents duplicate business requests; repeated keys with different amounts must be rejected.

Statuses: PENDING, PROCESSING, SUCCESS, FAILED, REVERSED. A local ledger debit is not proof that an external cash dispenser or bank paid successfully.

questions.question: Practice
questions.answer: Run two sessions against a disposable InnoDB database. Hold the account row lock in session one; verify session two waits. Commit session one, then verify session two reads the updated balance. Test insufficient funds, inactive accounts, duplicate requests and a failure before commit.

summary: Two withdrawal requests compete for the same ₹5,000 account balance. Follow both requests from the controller to their final ledger and audit records.
example_label: Illustrative production scenario — fictional educational records

paragraphs: Account 101 belongs to the illustrative customer Rahul Sharma and holds ₹5,000. Request 7001 asks for ₹5,000; request 7002 asks for ₹10,000. Both arrive within milliseconds. They are separate authorized business requests, not duplicate deliveries.

The ₹10,000 request cannot succeed even if it acquires the lock first. In the illustrated order, request 7001 acquires the account lock first, commits its debit, and request 7002 then reads ₹0. The application must never decide from an earlier unlocked balance.

This lesson models an internal ledger withdrawal. Cash dispensing or an external bank debit would require an additional externally confirmed payment workflow; a local SUCCESS does not prove cash was delivered.
Large-population examples show representative rows, not all 2,000 or 10,000 records. Run totals refer to the complete illustrative population, not the displayed subset.
